title: Case study: energy supply in Namibia

blocks.heading: The case study: energy supply in Namibia
blocks.text: What Namibia's energy supply consists of, why it is that way, and how it is changing - a country whose geography shapes every part of its supply.

blocks.heading: Namibia: what the supply is
blocks.text: Namibia's largest domestic power station is the hydro plant at Ruacana, on the Kunene River in the far north-west, with a capacity of about 340 megawatts (2010s figure). Most of the rest of the country's generating need is not generated at home: roughly half of Namibia's electricity was imported in the 2010s (rounded), from the grids of neighbouring countries. Solar farms have been added since the mid-2010s, sensible in a country with more than 3 000 hours of sunshine a year.

blocks.heading: Why the supply is this way
blocks.text: The chain runs from geography to supply. The population is small - about 2.5 million - and thinly spread, so the domestic market is too small to repay many large power stations. The country's rivers are mostly dry or seasonal; the Kunene, on the Angolan border, is one of the few with reliable flow worth damming, which is why Ruacana sits there. Importing from neighbouring grids has cost less than building large new stations, so imports filled the gap. And the sunshine is abundant, which is why solar generation, cheap to run once the farms are built because it needs no fuel, is the fastest-growing domestic source.

blocks.heading: The judgement the case study teaches
blocks.text: Namibia shows the trade-offs of 3.5.1 in one place. Imports cost money that leaves the country and leave supply dependent on neighbours, so the country gains by generating more at home. But new stations are expensive to build, and the market is small, so each plant must fit what the country can repay. Solar fits that test: its building costs per unit have fallen, its running costs are low because no fuel is bought, and the resource - sunshine - is the best in the region. The result is a supply moving from imports and one hydro station towards solar, without pretending the transition is free.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Connects to 3.1 Development (a small market limits what can be built), to 3.6 Water (hydro depends on a reliable river), and back to 3.5.1: the benefits and disadvantages of renewable energy, weighed for one real country.
